headline: Plum Gut on the Neap: Bass Come Out After Dark, Porgies Never Left
subhead: Steady scup and blackfish on the reefs, bass playing hard to get till the sun drops — and the water's finally soft enough to fish slow again.
body_markdown:
Had a young fella stop me at the ramp in Mattituck the other morning, tackle still tagged from the shop, asking why he couldn't buy a striper bite at ten in the morning off Horton Point. I told him what my father told me — fish don't own a watch, but they do own a thermometer. Sixty years I've watched this shoreline, and every July it's the same lesson relearned: when the water goes soft and warm the way it has this month, the big bass quit feeding on the clock and start feeding on the light. Or the lack of it.

That's exactly what's happening right now. The Sound's carrying a real gradient this week — warmer up toward the western reaches, cooling off as you swing east toward the Race, with New London running a good two degrees under what Kings Point's showing. Out here on the North Fork we're sitting in between, and the water off Rocky Point and Horton has that thick, milky-green July look to it that tells you the bait's been in tight and the bass have had their fill during the day. So they're sliding into ambush mode — dawn, dusk, full dark — working the rips and current seams where the bait gets pinned rather than chasing it out in open water under the sun.

Plum Gut's been the honest word this week. Boats working the tide changes at first light have been picking up slot fish and the occasional overslot working bucktails — three-quarter to one-ounce — bounced along the bottom where the rip folds over itself on the edge of the reef. Nothing that'll make you call your buddy screaming, but steady enough that a patient rod isn't going home skunked. After dark, eels and soft plastic swimbaits swum slow through the same water have been the better producers, and that's not an accident — bass sitting in a strong current don't want to chase, they want the bait to come to them.

Here's the piece worth paying attention to: we're heading into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, and that's going to ease the current speed through the Gut and the rips off Orient over the next several days. I've fished this pattern more times than I can count — when the tide slacks off from those big spring runs, the bite window actually widens. You don't need to be standing there at the exact peak of the moving water anymore. Lighter jigs, slower retrieves, more patience — that's the move. If you've been fishing three-quarter ounce bucktails, drop to a half. Let it hang a little longer in the seam instead of ripping it through.

Fluke, porgy, and blackfish have been the meat and potatoes out here and I won't oversell them because they don't need it — they've just been quietly good, week after week. Porgies on the reef structure off Rocky Point and out toward Orient have been thick, taking sandworms and green crab on standard hi-lo rigs in twenty to thirty-five feet, no real trick to it, just find the rock piles and drop straight down. Blackfish are mixed in on the same structure, crab baits working best, though the real tog fishing won't heat up proper till fall — right now it's a bonus fish while you're chasing scup. Fluke have been solid drifting the sand-to-structure edges off Mattituck Inlet and along the flats toward Horton, four-inch white Gulp on a bucktail teaser rig doing the damage on the moving water, better on the last two hours of the ebb when the bait gets pushed out of the inlet mouth.

Weakfish — and I say this carefully because that stock's had some lean years — have started showing again on the calm, warm evenings, a few keeper-class fish mixed in with the fluke drifts near the inlet mouths. We figured that rebuild might happen if the weather stayed settled, and it looks like it's starting to. Small sample size, but worth keeping an eye on if you're out there at last light with soft plastics.

Bluefish have mostly stayed offshore of us so far, chopping bunker pods along the beaches to our west, but I wouldn't be shocked to see that push our way — when those bunker schools finally work up the Sound proper, the blues follow, and Horton Point and Rocky Point both have the structure to hold them once they arrive.

We also flagged last week that this stretch could see some early bonito scouting activity as the water kept climbing, riding the same warmth that's been pushing albies and bonito around Montauk and the Vineyard. Haven't had a confirmed fish yet in my water, but the conditions are lining up — if you're working the Orient side and see nervous bait getting pushed on the surface in calm early morning light, don't assume it's just blues. Worth a few casts with a small metal to check.

Looking ahead: with the neap easing the current and the moon going quiet, I'd fish the low-light windows at Plum Gut and Orient with patience over horsepower, keep the porgy gear rigged for the slow stretches, and watch that inlet water at dusk for weakfish and maybe that first bonito surprise. Nothing here is a sure thing, but the pattern's honest, and honest is what this stretch of water has always rewarded.
